title: GPU Fleet, Capacity & CI/CD Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes Redwood's standard approach for managing GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC module patterns, and our CI/CD/build pipelines used to deliver inference infrastructure. It is intended for infra engineers, SRE, and platform owners who operate or modify GPU-backed services.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Provide a single reference for day-0 and day-2 activities that keep the GPU fleet healthy, predictable, and secure.
- Scope: GPU capacity planning, pool definitions, autoscaling policies, IaC module usage, CI/CD flows for infra modules and runtime images, runbooks for common incidents, and on-call responsibilities. Does not replace service-level runbooks for individual model-serving stacks.

Ownership and contacts:
- Owner team: engineering (Infra & SRE shared ownership).
- Primary owners: Aisha Patel (Infra Lead), Marco Li (GPU Fleet PM).
- On-call escalation: see team on-call rota and escalation playbook.

High-level architecture and inventory:
- GPU pools are organized by zone, instance type, and workload class:
  - pooled-general (T4/A10G equivalent) — best-effort, low-priority training/test workloads
  - pooled-low-latency (A100/H100 equivalent) — latencysensitive production inference
  - reserved-dedicated — reserved capacity for Dedicated customers (SLA-backed)
- Each pool is represented by a Terraform module that manages ASGs/GKE node pools and capacity reservations where supported.
- Networking: Each pool connects to the VPC through regional subnets with egress NAT gateways per account and strict egress ACLs for telemetry and container registry access.

Capacity planning and Sizing:
1) Quarterly capacity review process:
   1. Gather 90/95/99th percentile token throughput and peak concurrent sessions per region (Telemetry team dashboard).
   2. Model workload mix (latency vs. throughput) and map to pool type.
   3. Add 20% cold-start buffer and 10% for maintenance/reservations.
   4. Produce commit request for cloud procurement or reserved capacity.
2) Warm pool sizing guidance:
   - Use historical p95 request size distribution to set target batch sizes for batching-aware workloads.
   - For low-latency pools, size for target p99 latency under nominal load with autoscaler headroom 30%.
3) Autoscaling policy templates (examples):
   - Throughput-driven (preferred for batch): scale based on tokens/sec metric with cool-down 120s.
   - Latency-driven: scale based on p95/p99 tail latency SLA with cooldown 60-120s.
   - Hybrid: min-instance floor + throughput spike detector + graceful scaling policy.

Terraform / IaC module patterns:
- Module layout (recommended):
  - modules/gpu-node-pool: manages cloud node pool + instance template + GPU drivers + node-labels
  - modules/gpu-scheduling: taints/tolerations, pod-affinity, preemption policy
  - modules/networking-eip: NAT/gateway and internal firewall rules per pool
  - modules/iam-roles: least-privilege roles for node bootstrap/telemetry
- Example usage snippet (Terraform HCL as a text example):
  ```hcl
  module "a100-low-latency" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.internal/infra/modules/gpu-node-pool.git//?ref=v1.4.0"
    region = "us-west1"
    instance_type = "a100-40gb"
    min_size = 4
    max_size = 40
    labels = { pool = "low-latency", env = "prod" }
  }
  ```
- Versioning: modules must be pinned with a semver tag and breaking changes require an ADR + migration guide.
- Tests: every module must include unit tests (terraform validate + checkov) and an integration smoke pipeline that provisions to a sandbox account.

CI/CD and build pipelines:
- Repos: infra-modules repo (monorepo for Terraform modules), infra-pipelines (shared pipeline code), gpu-runtime-images (Dockerfiles and bake configs).
- CI checks (required):
  - terraform fmt/validate, tflint, checkov, dependency scan
  - terraform-plan must be human-approved for production workspaces
  - module release: automated changelog + semver bump + git tag on merge to main
- CD patterns:
  - Sandbox: automatic plan & apply on merge to main using sandbox workspace.
  - Staging: gated apply triggered by approvals and passing integration smoke tests.
  - Production: apply via runbook deployment (manual trigger) with preflight checks and rollback plan.
- Image build & registry:
  - Base images baked from approved Packer templates (shared inventory).
  - GPU drivers installed at image-build time, drivers version tracked in module variables.
  - Registry: artifacts stored in private registry at registry.redwood.internal with manifest signing.
  - Image promotion flow: build -> integration -> staging -> prod promotion tags.

Operational runbooks (top-level summaries):
- GPU node unreachable / driver mismatch:
  1. Detect: alert fires when node kubelet NotReady or driver version mismatch > 30% nodes.
  2. Mitigation: cordon node, drain, and check kernel logs (/var/log/nvidia-driver-install.log). If systematic, revert driver package in image and roll nodes.
  3. Postmortem: collect node-exporter and driver install logs, create incident PR.
- Autoscaler runaway (scale-to-zero/rapid flapping):
  1. Detect: scaling events > 10 in 10m or sudden drop in healthy pods.
  2. Mitigation: pause autoscaler, revert policy, and scale to safe floor (min_instances).
  3. Follow-up: adjust thresholds and add smoothing to metric pipeline.
- Out-of-capacity clouds/region outage:
  1. Failover: routing policy routes new requests to secondary region/pool class.
  2. Capacity request: activate reserved burst-capacity account and notify capacity-oncall.
  3. Customer impact: if Dedicated capacity impacted, follow customer SLA playbook and notify commercial.

Day-2 operations and housekeeping:
- Regular tasks (weekly/monthly):
  - Weekly: verify image driver matrix and run smoke tests across each pool.
  - Monthly: reclaim idle nodes > 72h unless tagged for debugging.
  - Quarterly: run capacity planning (see section above).
- Cost controls: use per-pool budgets and alerting on forecasted monthly spend > 10% budget.

Security & networking considerations:
- Network segmentation: each pool has a dedicated subnet and egress NAT gateway with least-privilege firewall rules.
- Secrets: node bootstrap uses KMS-wrapped secrets; workloads must use workload identity with short-lived credentials.
- Audit: terraform state stored in encrypted remote backend with restricted ACLs; module releases require 2 approvers for prod-impacting changes.

Onboarding checklist for new infra engineers:
1) Access: cloud account, git, registry, pager duty, Slack channels.
2) Run the sandbox module integration test locally.
3) Review the GPU fleet dashboard and SLOs.
4) Shadow on-call for two weeks.

Change and rollout guidance:
- Rolling driver or image updates: use canary pool (5% capacity) -> monitor p95/p99 and error rates for 1-2 hours -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%. Abort on deviation threshold (error increase > 2x or p99 increase > 30%).
- Terraform breaking changes: publish ADR, create migration plan, and provide a migration job that updates live resources in a controlled manner.

Appendices and references:
- Relevant pages: see related_pages above.
- Examples: driver compatibility matrix table and common RPM/DEB packages are maintained in the infra repo under docs/driver-matrix.md.
- Troubleshooting checklist and diagnostics commands are available in the runbooks directory.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: Created (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-02-15: Updated autoscaler templates and CI gating policy (Marco Li).

If you are making changes that affect production capacity, contact the capacity-oncall channel and follow the production rollout section before applying changes.
